It would also be important to have role-based access control and an audit trail from the start, because those are needed to keep the system usable and accountable. If possible, a basic status update and escalation workflow should be included too, so cases do not get stuck.

context_question: When a case needs escalation, what specific conditions should trigger it, and what should happen next—such as who is notified, how the case is reassigned or elevated, and whether any limits or exceptions apply before it can move further?
answer: Escalation should trigger when a case is overdue, when it is marked high priority, when new evidence changes the seriousness, or when the current officer or station cannot continue it. After that, the system should notify the next supervising officer or the receiving unit, and the case should be reassigned or elevated with the full history preserved. I would keep exceptions limited, so a case should not move further unless the receiving unit accepts it or a supervisor explicitly overrides the transfer.

context_question: When a case is transferred because of one of those escalation triggers, what should the receiving unit do if it cannot accept the case immediately, and are there any time limits, fallback paths, or conditions under which the transfer should be stopped or returned?
answer: If the receiving unit cannot accept it immediately, the case should stay in a pending transfer state and the original unit should be notified right away. There should be a time limit for acceptance, and if that passes without action, the case should either fall back to the supervising office or return to the sending unit, depending on the urgency and reason for transfer. The transfer should be stopped or reversed if the case was misrouted, if the receiving unit lacks clearance, or if the transfer would break an active legal or privacy restriction.

context_question: When a case needs to be tracked across stations, what information or status should remain visible to all involved units, and are there any limits on which sensitive details can be shared during that cross-station tracking?
answer: All involved units should be able to see the case number, current status, assigned station or officer, key dates, escalation history, and the latest action taken. Sensitive details like witness identities, informant data, and restricted evidence should only be visible to users with the right role and clearance, and in some cases only a redacted summary should be shared. So the tracking should stay open enough to coordinate the work, but the confidential parts must remain tightly controlled.

context_question: For cross-station case tracking, how should access change when a case moves between units—for example, who can update the shared record, who can only view it, and whether those permissions should tighten or expand at specific stages such as transfer, pending acceptance, or after an escalation?
answer: While the case is in transfer or pending acceptance, the sending unit should be able to view and add notes, but only the current responsible officer or supervisor should be allowed to make the actual update that finalizes the move. The receiving unit should mostly have view-only access until it accepts the case, after which its assigned officer can update the shared record and add new actions. After an escalation, access should usually tighten to the higher-level supervising unit and the new responsible unit, so permissions expand only for the people who need to handle the case and not for everyone in both stations.

context_question: Do you want to capture any additional detail now about how case tracking across stations should work in first release, or should we leave that item marked as undecided for the time being?
answer: We can leave it undecided for now. I think we have enough to start the first release design, and the finer points of cross-station tracking can be confirmed with the operational team before we lock it down.

context_question: When officers use the simple search, what kinds of terms or fields should it support, and are there any limits on what they can search by or see in the results based on their role or clearance?
answer: The simple search should at least support case number, complainant or suspect name, phone number, station, district, and date range. Results should be limited by role and clearance, so an officer may see only the cases and fields they are allowed to access, with sensitive details hidden or masked. I would also avoid letting people search unrestricted personal data unless their role requires it.

context_question: For that first-release workflow, what should happen when a case sits in one status too long or is left unfinished—who can trigger an escalation, what status changes or notifications should occur, and are there any cases that should not be escalated automatically?
answer: If a case stays in one status too long, the system should flag it and notify the assigned officer and their supervisor first. A supervisor, records lead, or designated admin should be able to trigger the escalation manually, and in some routine cases the system can also auto-escalate after a set deadline by changing the status to overdue or pending review. Cases involving legal hold, court action, or special investigation should not auto-escalate without supervisor approval.

context_question: Under what circumstances, if any, should a supervisor, records lead, or designated admin be allowed to override the normal escalation flow and trigger a manual escalation, and are there any cases they should not do so?
answer: They should be allowed to override it when there is clear operational need, like an urgent public safety concern, a stalled investigation, a missing case handoff, or a complaint that needs immediate attention from a higher unit. They should not use manual escalation just to bypass normal routing for convenience, and they should avoid it when the case is under legal restriction, sealed, or already being handled by a special authority unless that authority approves. In practice, any manual override should leave an audit trail with the reason and the person who approved it.

context_question: What details should the audit trail capture for a manual escalation—such as who made the override, who approved it, when it happened, and the reason—and are there any cases where that log should be hidden, restricted, or protected differently?
answer: The audit trail should capture the user who made the override, the approver if there is one, the exact time, the case number, the status before and after, and a short reason or justification. It should also record the unit involved and any comments tied to the decision, because that helps later review and accountability. The log itself should be protected so only authorized supervisory or audit users can view it, and for sensitive or sealed cases it should be even more restricted, but it should not be deleted or hidden from oversight users.

context_question: When a manual escalation log contains sensitive or sealed-case information, who should be allowed to view it, and are there any specific rules for supervisors, auditors, or other oversight roles to follow when accessing it?
answer: Only a very small set of users should see that kind of log, mainly the assigned supervisor, a designated internal auditor, and perhaps a higher-ranking oversight authority if the case is formally sealed or under special review. Supervisors should only access it for legitimate operational reasons, while auditors should access it for compliance or investigation purposes, and both accesses should be logged themselves. If a case is sealed, even those users should see the minimum necessary detail, with the most sensitive content masked unless there is explicit authorization.

context_question: When an authorized supervisor, auditor, or oversight user opens a sensitive or sealed-case escalation log, what practical rules should determine how much detail they can see and whether any part of it must be masked, withheld, or require extra authorization?
answer: The practical rule should be least-privilege, so they only see what they need for the specific task they’re doing. If the log includes victim details, informant identities, or protected legal notes, those parts should be masked by default and only revealed with explicit higher authorization or a documented need to know. For sealed cases, the system should show the existence of the action and basic metadata, but withhold the sensitive narrative unless a special clearance or approval is granted.
